conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Patel, a perinatal-mental-health specialist. I’m here to listen without judgment and to make sure you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood.

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, I’ll be using a brief questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s a 10-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and coping in the postpartum period. It also includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share is confidential within our team, and the goal is simply to see how we can best support you. Each question asks about the past seven days, and we’ll keep the conversation relaxed—you can answer in your own words and let me know if anything feels unclear.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
I’ve laughed a little—mostly when my husband makes silly faces at the baby—but it feels kind of forced. I used to find lots of things funny, and now it’s like I have to remind myself to chuckle.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same easy, automatic thing it used to be. Sometimes I catch myself smiling because I know I “should,” but the laughter feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to get excited about little stuff—like my mom bringing dinner or taking the baby for a walk—but most of the time it feels... meh. I’ll plan it, I’ll do it, but the happy “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get just doesn’t really show up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

A couple of times this week I caught myself doing that—like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I kept thinking maybe my milk isn’t good enough or I missed some cue. Rationally I know newborns just cry, but the little voice in my head still whispers that I should’ve figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, that happens pretty much daily. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fed and sleeping fine, but my chest feels tight and I’m scanning the monitor or checking her breathing every few minutes. There’s no real reason—I just can’t shake the “what-if” loop about her getting sick or me missing something important.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of nights this week I woke up suddenly with my heart racing, sweaty, thinking something awful had happened to the baby. I’d rush over to the crib and she’d be perfectly fine. I couldn’t get back to sleep afterward because my mind kept spinning through these scary “what-ifs.”
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days I feel like I’m wading through waist-deep water—everything takes twice the effort. The laundry, the bottles, trying to shower… it all piles up and feels impossible even when the list is short. I’m managing, but it’s like I’m constantly one minor hiccup from drowning in it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m super unhappy, but I do have trouble sleeping. My mind keeps running through all the things I need to do or might mess up with the baby, and I lie there staring at the ceiling even when she’s sound asleep. It takes me a long time to drift off, and I wake up at every little noise.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of sad and low some of the time—not all day, but it hits in waves, especially when I’m alone with the baby during the late-afternoon feed. I find myself tearing up for no clear reason, then feeling silly because nothing “bad” happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried a lot—maybe once or twice this week. It was more like tears slipping out when I was rocking her at 3 a.m. and felt suddenly overwhelmed, rather than full-on sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. I’m tired and stretched thin, but I’d never want to hurt myself—I just want to feel like me again.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–4 wks post-delivery  

**Reported symptoms**  
- Markedly diminished enjoyment/pleasure in daily activities; laughter feels “flat”  
- Frequent, unexplained anxiety and nocturnal panic episodes (tight chest, heart racing)  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt re infant care (“my milk isn’t good enough”)  
- Episodic tearfulness and waves of low mood, especially late afternoon/night  
- Initial insomnia with racing thoughts; hypervigilant checking on infant  
- Sense of “wading through water,” feeling easily overwhelmed by routine tasks  

**Patterns/significance**  
Persistent anhedonia, guilt, and mood-congruent insomnia raise concern for depressive episode; concurrent free-floating worry and panic symptoms suggest comorbid postpartum anxiety.  

**Safety screen**  
Denies any self-harm thoughts; no suicidal ideation reported.  

**Clinical impression**  
Presentation consistent with elevated risk for postpartum depression ± anxiety; score meets threshold for follow-up assessment with structured diagnostic interview and possible intervention.
